# Generative UI Ep.1 — Live, Real-Time Generation

**Platform:** Instagram (The Point of Interface) · **Series:** Part 1 of 3 on generative UI · **Target runtime:** about 1:50 (over the original 60-90 sec; tighten or split if you want it under 90)

**Premise:** Generative UI splits into two types — runtime (adaptive, dynamic UI) and build-time (UI generated by an LLM, then deployed). Part 1 covers runtime: not a new idea, but reshaped recently by agentic interfaces and AI trends. We look at Meta, Google Search, and Spotify, then land on two reasons it matters — accessibility and personalization.

## Intro (0:00-0:12)

On-camera: "Hi, I'm Zac, and this is The Point of Interface, a design series about how interfaces get made and where they're headed. We're starting with generative UI. This is a three-part series where we'll cover different aspects of it, go deeper on its applications, and look at what it means for us as designers."

Visual: Zac on camera with the retro-sci-fi Point of Interface title card. Quick montage of three interfaces reshaping themselves (a feed, a search results page, a chat) to set up the topic, ending on a series card: "Generative UI, Part 1 of 3."

## Defining generative UI: two types (0:12-0:30)

On-camera: "So what is generative UI? Broadly speaking, it comes in two types. The first is runtime: the interface is adaptive and dynamic, changing as you use it. The second is build time: a large language model, most likely, generates the interface, and then it gets deployed. Both have changed a lot in the last couple of years, because of agentic interfaces, broader trends in AI and technology, and how consumers behave."

Beat: "Let's start with runtime."

Visual: Two-panel card. Left, "Runtime": a feed's components rearranging in real time. Right, "Build time": a prompt turning into a finished app that then ships. Highlight the left panel as today's focus and dim the right.

## Not a new idea: Meta and Google (0:30-0:55)

On-camera: "Runtime generative UI isn't new. Social media companies have been adapting their interfaces for a really long time. Take the Meta feed: a lot of the components are custom to the algorithm. It serves you different types of content, and that content arrives in different interface formats. It's a dynamic way of pushing different kinds of interaction to the user."

Visual: Screen recording of your own Meta feed, scrolling slowly. Outline each post format as it passes (photo, reel, ad, suggested account) with a label: "same feed, different components." Blur anything personal.

On-camera: "We're seeing more of it in search, too. Google Search has done this for a while. Type in a number and you get a calculator. That part may not use a large language model at all, but it's still a generative interface. Now, with AI Mode, it can do more: fetch and summarize different kinds of information, and sometimes present it in components that are easy to click."

Visual: Screen recording in Google Search. Type a number and show the calculator appear, then run a query in AI Mode and highlight the clickable components in the answer.

## Why it's good: accessibility (0:55-1:20)

On-camera: "So why is real-time generative UI a good thing? The first reason is accessibility. We don't design for everybody. As designers, we tend to design for the people we think will use the app the most, and the people who get less of that attention are often people with a visual or motor impairment, whose experience of the same application can be very different."

On-camera: "Researchers have been working on this for a long time. In 2004, Krzysztof Gajos and his collaborators introduced SUPPLE, a system that generated interfaces around a person's abilities, devices and preferences. The goal wasn't engagement. It was giving people with motor impairments an interface that actually worked for them."

Beat: "A generative interface can meet each person where they are, instead of us guessing who the average user is."

Visual: Title card "SUPPLE, 2004" with a lower-third credit (Gajos, Weld, Wobbrock). Animate three redrawn versions of the same dialog box: standard, enlarged for impaired dexterity, high-contrast for low vision. Redraw them rather than lifting figures from the papers.

## Why it's good: personalization (1:20-1:40)

On-camera: "The second reason is personalization. What gets personalized, and which personalization suits which audience, is a bigger conversation. It's a research question and a technical question. But look across Meta, Google Search and even Spotify, and you can see how an interface that changes dynamically based on the data it collects can create really interesting experiences. Spotify Wrapped, for example, may not be real-time generation, but it shows how different data streams can create content that feeds into the user's experience."

Visual: Side-by-side Spotify Wrapped-style cards for different listeners: same format, different data. Use your own Wrapped screens, or redrawn generic data cards. Overlay text: "same format, different data."

## Outro / tease (1:40-1:50)

On-camera: "That's runtime generative UI: interfaces that adapt as you use them. In the next two parts, we'll go deeper on its applications, including the build-time side, and on what all of this means for us as designers."

Visual: End card with the series title and a "Part 1 of 3" marker. Quick teaser flash of a prompt turning into a finished app (build time).

## Parked for later parts

- Chat-canvas generation (Claude and ChatGPT artifacts) versus localized dynamic components on traditional pages. Full-page generative UI breaks structural consistency, so most sites localize it, while self-contained chat interfaces can go fully generative.
- The trade-off between structure and personalization.
- Gajos's adaptive-UI findings: accuracy mattered more than predictability for performance (CHI 2008), but adaptive interfaces can take more mental effort than researchers expected.
- Build time: vibe-coded websites, static (pre-deployment) versus live generation, and the trade-offs of letting AI choose components versus designing by hand.
